title: Australia needs an AI 'early warning system', top cyber security chief warns
full_text:
Australia needs an artificial intelligence "early warning system" to help defend against the dangers of the increasingly powerful technology, according to the nation's cyber intelligence chief.
Australian Signals Directorate director-general Abigail Bradshaw also urged Australian organisations to embrace AI for its defensive capabilities, saying it was one of the crucial tools that the nation needed to protect itself.
It comes as Australian politicians and AI company executives respond to a growing international chorus of warnings the race to develop AI could outstrip humanity's ability to control it.
Speaking at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute's (ASPI) Sydney Dialogue AI Masterclass on Monday, Ms Bradshaw said intelligence and security agencies needed to work with AI companies to identify early risks.
"What we are missing at the moment, which we have in a cyber context but we don't yet have it formalised in an AI context, is an early warning system," she said.
Ms Bradshaw said bringing together reports of individual incidents would help identify wider patterns, adding that these risks extended beyond cyber security to areas such as biotechnology.
The public servant, who is tasked with Australia's cyber offensive capabilities, balanced the warning with a more optimistic assessment about AI capabilities helping those tasked with defence.
She pointed to existing cyber partnerships between government and industry, and international arrangements for quickly sharing technical information.
Australian government agencies had been granted access to major AI companies' cutting-edge models that were limited from wide release.
She confirmed that this included Anthropic's Mythos, which was temporarily restricted after the US government placed it under an export control, and OpenAI's cyber versions of their models.
Ms Bradshaw said her agency used this access to help Australian organisations fortify their system and identify potential vulnerabilities.
"What would have taken cybersecurity experts in ASD weeks and weeks of work has been done in hours," she said.
Ms Bradshaw urged organisations to maintain basic security measures while using AI to defend their networks.
Defenders needed capabilities on par with those available to cybercriminals and state-backed attackers, she said.
In a separate panel on Monday, Australia's AI Safety Institute general manager Kate Conroy urged companies and agencies to let their teams, or their staff, experiment with advanced AI.
"If you don't already have it your teams are probably already doing it in their free time," she said.
Calls for global AI slowdown
In July, more than a thousand employees of leading AI companies signed onto an open letter which called for the US government to step in to help pave the way for an AI development slowdown.
In the past week the high-profile resignation of Anthropic staffer Jacob Coxon and an essay published by the company's chief executive reignited a global conversation over a global slowdown effort.
Australia's assistant science minister Andrew Charlton told the ASPI conference that Australia should help shape the response.
"I am not in favour of leaving it to the companies and I'm not in favour of leaving it to the superpowers," he said.
Mr Charlton said governments should assume AI would keep becoming more capable, given companies' financial incentives, and despite executives discussing slowing down.
OpenAI vice-president of global policy Ann O'Leary told the event the company was working with governments and AI safety bodies, such as Australia's AI Safety Institute, as well as providing models for review before release.
But, she said, the absence of wider laws slowing development meant OpenAI and other companies were employing their own voluntary co-ordination efforts to "pace" progress.
Ms O'Leary said OpenAI was eager to train its AI models in Australia, saying it was in talks with the federal government about copyright.
"We are deep in conversation with the Australian government about these questions," she said.
"You have caught our attention."
